script.opening: "My dad died of bowel cancer in his early 40s, and a couple of other relatives had it young too. The hospital told my family it runs in the genes. I’m 22 and I’m worried — do I need to be tested or screened? Am I going to get it too?"

facts.text: Dad, Mark, died at 43 of bowel cancer, 3 years ago. His sister (Daniel’s aunt) had "her bowel removed" in her thirties. Grandad died "of his bowels" young. "I don’t know all the details. They were young, like him." The hospital told Mum it was genetic; Mum has a letter somewhere with the name of the condition.
Never had a genetic test, a camera test or a referral. Was 19 when Dad died and "didn’t want to know then".
No bleeding, no change in bowel habit, no tummy pain, no weight loss, not tired. Feels completely well.
No medicines, no allergies. Non-smoker; drinks at weekends. Had a lump removed from his jaw at 15 ("a bony lump — they said harmless"), only if asked about other lumps or operations.
Younger sister, Ellie (17), and brother, Sam (14). Mum is well. Has a girlfriend of 2 years; they talk about having children one day. Works as a trainee electrician.
"It’s hard. I think about it a lot." Low at times since Dad died, never thoughts of self-harm. Has been putting this off.

Quiet, serious, a little nervous. Ask "And would I have it?", "So I could stop it happening to me?" and "What if I’d rather not know?" Ask whether you should tell your brother and sister. Respond well to honest, clear information and a concrete plan.

ice.ideas: "It runs in the family, so I’ll probably get it."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "That I’ll die young like him." Also worried about passing it on to children, and whether his 14-year-old brother is at risk now.
ice.expectations: "To know if I need testing or screening."

cues: "The hospital told my family it runs in the genes" — an inherited syndrome; ask for the letter and details.
"What if I’d rather not know?" — testing is his choice; explore it.
"Should I tell my brother and sister?" — family implications, including a 14-year-old.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a likely INHERITED colorectal-cancer syndrome (FAP/Lynch) from the strong early-onset family history and that it warrants a PRIORITY clinical-genetics referral (no surveillance yet at 22, when FAP colonoscopy starts at 12–14)
Explains FAP’s AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT inheritance (50% risk to offspring; APC gene; hundreds of polyps from adolescence; near-100% lifetime risk if untreated)
Discusses PRESYMPTOMATIC GENETIC testing (often for a known family mutation) and refers to CLINICAL GENETICS, respecting the right to know/not know and mentioning the ABI Code on insurance
Outlines the SURVEILLANCE/management for carriers (colonoscopy from age 12–14 per BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG 2020, prophylactic colectomy, upper-GI surveillance) and that it dramatically reduces cancer death

Distinguishes LYNCH syndrome (fewer polyps, endometrial/other cancers; aspirin per NICE NG151) and MUTYH-associated polyposis, and recognises that symptomatic suspected colorectal cancer would follow the NICE NG12 pathway
Supports an anxious young person, respects his autonomy over testing, and checks understanding

Explores the impact of his father’s early death and his fears for his own future and any future children, and discusses the implications for relatives (cascade testing) sensitively, with his consent to share

Safety-nets and follows up: clinical-genetics referral, surveillance information, assessment/NICE NG12 referral if bowel symptoms, and review — the inherited-syndrome pathway, not dismissal or an inappropriate suspected cancer pathway referral

worked.txt: "You were absolutely right to come. A strong family history of bowel cancer at a young age, described as running in the family, points to an inherited condition — and the good news is that identifying it early means we can prevent the cancer."

"One likely condition is FAP — a fault in a gene that causes lots of bowel polyps from the teens, which can turn cancerous. It’s passed on in a dominant way, so there’s a one-in-two chance of inheriting it from an affected parent."

"Often the family’s exact gene fault is known, so you can have a blood test for it. I’ll refer you to the genetics service today and mark it as a priority, because in FAP families camera checks usually start in the early teens. Whether to be tested is your choice — some want to know, some don’t — and they’ll guide you through it. In the UK, insurers can’t ask for a predictive gene test result, apart from one rare condition."
"If you do carry it, regular camera tests from a young age and, often, removing the bowel before cancer develops are hugely effective — they save lives. That’s exactly why finding out is worthwhile."
"Have you had any bowel symptoms — bleeding, change in habit, weight loss? … No. If you ever do, tell me, as that would need separate urgent assessment."

"This is a lot at 22, and I’m here to support you. Other relatives may be at risk too — the genetics team can help you decide how to share it, and it’s your information. I’ll get the genetics referral going, and we’ll go through whatever they advise together."

f.learning: A strong family history of EARLY-onset bowel cancer across relatives, described as hereditary, suggests an inherited colorectal-cancer syndrome — notably FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS (FAP) or Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) — and warrants a priority clinical-genetics referral (BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG 2020); MUTYH-associated polyposis (autosomal recessive) and attenuated FAP are other possibilities. FAP (APC gene) is AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT, causing hundreds-to-thousands of colonic ADENOMATOUS POLYPS from adolescence with a near-100% lifetime colorectal-cancer risk if untreated, and extra-colonic features (duodenal/desmoid tumours, CHRPE, osteomas, thyroid); each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the faulty gene. Discuss PRESYMPTOMATIC GENETIC testing (often the family’s causative mutation is known and can be tested for) via clinical genetics, counselling that testing is the patient’s choice (right to know/not know, psychological and practical implications; ABI Code 2018 on insurance; cascade testing of relatives with consent, GMC Confidentiality 2017) and that early identification enables life-saving surveillance. For confirmed carriers, management is intensive surveillance and prevention — colonoscopy from age 12 to 14, usually prophylactic COLECTOMY when polyp burden warrants (late teens or early adulthood), and upper-GI (duodenal) surveillance — which dramatically reduces colorectal-cancer death. Distinguish LYNCH syndrome (far fewer polyps, earlier-onset colorectal cancer, and associated endometrial and other cancers, with its own surveillance including daily aspirin per NICE NG151 and gynae advice). Support the anxious young person, respect autonomy, and refer to clinical genetics; if the patient has bowel SYMPTOMS, assess and refer via the NICE NG12 pathway for symptomatic suspected colorectal cancer, with FIT where indicated — but an asymptomatic inherited-risk screening request follows the priority genetics pathway, not a suspected cancer pathway referral.

knowledge.guideline: [1] BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG guidelines for the management of hereditary colorectal cancer (Monahan et al., Gut 2020) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE NG151 (colorectal cancer, 2020) · [3] NICE HTG430 (formerly DG27; molecular testing strategies for Lynch syndrome in people with colorectal cancer, 2017) · [5] ABI Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance (2018) · [6] GMC Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information (2017)
knowledge.summary: Bowel cancer in a father in his early 40s and other young relatives, labelled hereditary by the hospital, points to an inherited syndrome such as familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) or Lynch syndrome. Refer promptly to clinical genetics, who can use the family’s known variant if there is one. In FAP, surveillance normally starts in early adolescence, so a 22-year-old who has had none needs prompt action. Testing is his choice. Ask about bowel symptoms, because symptoms need the usual suspected-cancer route.

points.t: Colorectal cancer at a young age in more than one relative, and a hospital statement that it runs in the family, suggest a hereditary syndrome. The commonest are Lynch syndrome and FAP; MUTYH-associated polyposis is another [1].

FAP is caused by a variant in the APC gene and is autosomal dominant: each child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it. Hundreds to thousands of adenomas develop from adolescence, and without treatment the lifetime colorectal cancer risk approaches 100%. Extra-colonic features include duodenal adenomas, desmoid tumours, osteomas, dental anomalies, congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium and thyroid cancer [1].

BSG/ACPGBI/UKCGG [1] advise colonoscopy for at-risk children in classical FAP families from age 12 to 14, with prophylactic colectomy timed by polyp burden, usually in late teens or early adulthood, and upper GI surveillance later. A young adult from a known FAP family who has had no surveillance needs prompt genetics and colonoscopy referral.

Also autosomal dominant, from mismatch repair gene variants. Fewer polyps but a high risk of colorectal, endometrial and other cancers. Colonoscopy surveillance starts at an age set by the gene [1]. NICE NG151 [2] recommends considering daily aspirin to reduce colorectal cancer risk in Lynch syndrome. Tumours of people with colorectal cancer are tested for Lynch syndrome (NICE HTG430, formerly DG27 [3]).
MUTYH-associated polyposis is autosomal recessive, so it usually affects siblings rather than parents and children. Genetics will clarify which syndrome applies to his family.

If the family variant is known, a predictive blood test can show whether he carries it. It is his choice, after genetic counselling. Insurers in the UK cannot ask for predictive test results, except Huntington’s disease for very large life policies (ABI Code 2018 [5]).

Rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, weight loss, abdominal pain or iron-deficiency anaemia need assessment in line with NICE NG12 [4], including FIT where indicated, regardless of the genetics referral.

model.text: Hello Mr Frost, I’m Dr Ahmed. What would you like to talk about today?

My dad died of bowel cancer in his early 40s, and a couple of other relatives had it young too. The hospital told my family it runs in the genes. I’m 22 and I’m worried. Do I need to be tested or screened? Am I going to get it too?

I’m very sorry about your dad. You’ve done exactly the right thing coming in. I’d like to understand the family history, check a couple of things about you, and then explain what this could mean and what we can do. Is that okay?
Yes.
Can you tell me about the relatives who had bowel cancer: which side of the family and how old they were?
I don’t know all the details. They were young, like him.
Did the hospital mention a particular name for the condition, or a gene test that found a fault in the family?
model.why: Establishes whether a family variant is known

model.text: I don’t know the details. Just that it’s genetic.
Has anyone ever offered you tests or a camera check of your bowel before?
model.why: Checks for missed cascade testing or surveillance

model.text: No, never.
Have you had any bleeding from your bottom, a change in your bowel habit, tummy pain, weight loss or tiredness?
model.why: Symptom screen for the NICE NG12 route

model.text: No, nothing.
How have things been for you since your dad died, and with all this on your mind?
It’s hard. I think about it a lot.
What do you understand about how it runs in families?
Just that I might have it too.
What worries you most, and what were you hoping I could do?
That I’ll die young like him. I want to know if I need testing or screening.

When bowel cancer affects several relatives at a young age and the hospital says it’s genetic, it usually means a gene fault is passed down. One possibility is familial adenomatous polyposis, or FAP, which causes lots of polyps in the bowel from the teenage years. Another is Lynch syndrome. The genetics team will work out which.
And would I have it?

With both of these, a parent with the fault passes it on to each child with a one in two chance. So you might have inherited it, and you might not. The really important thing is that if you do carry it, regular camera tests and, in FAP, removing the bowel before cancer starts can prevent the cancer. Knowing gives you control.
model.why: Explains 50% inheritance and that surveillance prevents cancer

model.text: So I could stop it happening to me?
That’s the aim, yes.

I’ll refer you to clinical genetics today, and mark it as a priority, because in FAP families checks usually start in the early teens. If the family fault is known, a blood test can show whether you have it. They’ll talk it through first, and whether you have the test is your decision.
model.why: Prompt genetics referral; predictive testing is his choice

model.text: What if I’d rather not know?

That’s your right. Genetics can still arrange camera checks based on the family history, so you’d be protected either way. And in the UK, insurers can’t ask you for a predictive gene test result, apart from one rare condition.
model.why: Respects the right not to know; addresses a common worry

model.text: That helps. Should I tell anyone else?
Other relatives may also be at risk. The genetics team can help you decide how to share it. It’s your information, and we’d support you with it.

While you wait, if you get any bleeding from your bottom, a change in your bowels, tummy pain or weight loss, come back straight away, because that would need checking separately and quickly. Let’s speak again once you’ve heard from genetics. Can you tell me what happens next?
model.why: Symptom safety net, follow-up and teach-back

model.text: You’re referring me to genetics, they’ll talk about a test and camera checks, and I come back if I get any bowel symptoms.
Exactly. And you can come and talk to me about any of it, including how you’re feeling about your dad.

social.t: His father’s early death shapes his fear. Offer support and bereavement services if he wants them.
Carrier status can affect decisions about relationships and children. Genetics services discuss reproductive options when relevant.

legal.t: Under the ABI Code on Genetic Testing and Insurance (2018), insurers cannot require or use predictive genetic test results, except for Huntington’s disease in life insurance over £500,000. Family history questions may still be asked.
His genetic information is confidential. Sharing it with relatives is his choice, with support; disclosure without consent is rarely justified (GMC Confidentiality 2017).

professional.t: Surveillance in FAP families usually starts in early adolescence. If he was never offered it, consider whether the family pathway broke down and act promptly; reflect or raise it as a learning event if appropriate.

community.t: UK polyposis registries and charities for bowel cancer and hereditary conditions offer information and peer support.

management.psychosocial: Bereavement support; right not to know; help with telling relatives.
sharedPlan: Predictive testing if the family variant is known, after counselling, his choice
Colonoscopy surveillance as advised by genetics
safetyNet: Bowel symptoms: return promptly for NICE NG12 assessment

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is a genetics conversation, not a cancer referral. The marks go to recognising the syndrome, acting promptly and leaving the choices with him.

items.fail: Sending a suspected-cancer referral or FIT kit for an asymptomatic man.
items.why: Hereditary risk is managed through genetics and surveillance.
items.fix: Refer to clinical genetics; use NICE NG12 only for symptoms.

items.why: FAP surveillance usually starts at 12–14; he has had none.
items.fix: Prioritise the referral and explain why.

items.why: Dominant conditions carry a 1 in 2 risk to each child.
